page_title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 3: TCP Basics & Handshake

summary.title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 3: TCP Basics & Handshake
summary.one_liner: You learn how TCP provides reliable, connection-oriented streaming over IP (sliding windows, sequence numbers, checksums, header fields and the SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK three-way handshake) and how to mock a handshake in a userspace stack.
takeaways: TCP is connection-oriented and streaming: it buffers data and reorders it before handing it to the application.
Sequence and acknowledgment numbers index the byte stream; the 20-byte header carries ports, flags, window size and checksum.
The handshake is SYN from client, SYN-ACK from server (ACK = seq + 1), then ACK from client; simultaneous open needs an extra exchange.
Initial sequence numbers must be hard to guess to prevent sequence number attacks; modern stacks generate them with more complex methods than a simple counter.
Options such as MSS, SACK, Window Scale and Timestamps extend the basic header.
summary.summary: The article is the third part of a series on building a userspace TCP/IP stack. It explains the reliability problems TCP solves, including sliding windows, flow and congestion control, and then covers TCP's basics such as streaming, packetization, checksums and full-duplex operation. It walks through the 20-byte TCP header and its flags, the three-way handshake with its open questions (ISN choice, simultaneous open, timeouts), and common TCP options. It ends by mocking a SYN-ACK response in the author's stack and testing it with nmap's SYN scan.
